statement: In 213 healthy volunteers aged 25 to 64 (108 women) who took LSD lying in a quiet hospital room with one investigator present, and placebo on another day in eight of the nine studies (nine double-blind crossover studies pooled by the Basel laboratory that ran them, 297 LSD sessions; one dose by mouth per session, 25 to 200 micrograms, as study conditions; Vizeli et al., 2024), the dose given was the strongest predictor of almost every effect compared with placebo, and characteristics measured before the dose were also associated with the response at a given dose: higher well-being rated just before, with stronger effects on most self-rated scales but not with a bad drug effect; anxiety rated just before, with more anxiety during the session; openness, with more mystical-type and oceanic ratings; extraversion, with more visual and auditory changes; more previous hallucinogen experience, with a smaller overall altered state and less anxious ego dissolution; and lower activity of the liver enzyme CYP2D6, with higher blood levels of LSD and more anxious ego dissolution. Neuroticism, agreeableness and conscientiousness predicted nothing. Older age went with more, and higher body weight with less, bad drug effect, and women had smaller increases than men in four positive ratings and in body temperature; the differences between women and men were not significant when one dose per study was analysed, and the abstract's statement that sex and body weight had no significant influence does not match the main results. The text gives the direction and significance of each association after correction for 551 tests but no sizes, which are only in a figure and a supplement not read here, so how much any characteristic other than dose matters cannot be said; bad drug effects were generally small. Expectations were not among the 19 predictors, and the setting barely varied. Bodies that differ (here the CYP2D6 enzyme) and earlier hallucinogen use are among the reasons people feel more or less from the same amount; everyone took one fixed dose per session, so what happens when someone who feels little takes more was not tested. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: In laboratory studies of healthy adults, the LSD dose mattered most for how strong the effects were. People who felt well just before had stronger effects, people who felt anxious had more anxiety, open personalities had more mystical feelings, and people who had used hallucinogens more often had a smaller overall effect. The paper gives the direction of each link but not its size. Everyone took one fixed dose, so what happens when someone who feels little takes more was not tested.

comparator: Volunteers with lower or higher values of each characteristic, at a given dose (placebo sessions in the same people in eight of nine studies)
outcome: Self-rated effects relative to placebo (visual analogue scales, 5D-ASC, MEQ30), blood pressure, heart rate, body temperature and blood LSD level
magnitude: Directions and corrected significance only; no sizes in the text. Dose strongest for every effect except body temperature (selected by LASSO for all 29 responses, largest for 21). Pre-dose well-being: stronger effects on most subjective scales, not bad drug effect; pre-dose anxiety: more 5D-ASC anxiety; openness: mystical-type and oceanic ratings; extraversion: visual and auditory changes; previous hallucinogen experience: smaller 5D-ASC total, less anxious ego dissolution; lower CYP2D6 activity: higher plasma LSD and more anxious ego dissolution; age more and body weight less bad drug effect; women smaller increases in four positive ratings and temperature (not significant in the sensitivity analysis).

statement: In 194 healthy, screened volunteers aged 18 to 45, four in five new to MDMA, who each took one capsule of MDMA lying in a quiet hospital ward in Basel, with a placebo on another day (10 double-blind crossover studies pooled by the laboratory that ran them; 125 mg for 164 people and 75 mg for 30, the same for women and men, as study conditions; Studerus et al., 2021), the amount taken per kilogram of body weight and the resulting blood level went most with how strongly the effects were felt, as the volunteers rated them. Without adjustment, the blood level was associated with the rating of any drug effect (standardized beta 0.48), and in penalized models dose per kilogram was selected for 21 of 25 effects and ranked first for 12, mostly pleasant and stimulating ones, but mattered less for unpleasant or anxious reactions. At the same dose per kilogram, lower activity of the liver enzyme CYP2D6 went with a higher blood level (beta −0.19), older age with a smaller rise in heart rate (−0.27), higher openness with more closeness to others (0.28) and oceanic boundlessness (0.22), higher neuroticism and trait anxiety, measured at screening, with more dread of ego dissolution (0.32 each) and impaired control (0.26 each), and a more anxious-depressed or introverted mood just before the capsule with more anxiety during the session (0.25 and 0.23); each explained 5 to 12% of the variation (semi-partial R2). For a rating of a bad drug effect, older age, trait anxiety and anxious-depressed mood before the dose ranked highest. Women and men did not differ once dose per kilogram was allowed for; because everyone took a fixed amount and women weighed less, women received more per kilogram, and this design cannot separate sex from dose per kilogram. Previous MDMA use showed no association, but no one had used it more than five times. Expectations were not among the measures, and the setting, the same for everyone, could not be studied. Bodies that differ are one reason people feel more or less from the same amount; everyone took one fixed dose, so what happens when someone who feels little takes more was not tested here (controlled studies of a second dose are covered in a separate answer). Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: In laboratory studies of healthy young adults, how much MDMA they got for their body weight, and how much reached the blood, went most with how strongly they felt it. People with more anxious personalities, or who felt anxious and low just before, had more anxiety during the session, and more open people felt closer to others. Women and men did not differ once body weight was allowed for. Everyone took one fixed amount, so what happens when someone who feels little takes more was not tested.

exposure: Characteristics measured before dosing: dose per kilogram and blood level, sex, age, CYP2D6 activity, previous MDMA use, personality and trait anxiety at screening, mood just before the dose
comparator: Volunteers with lower or higher values of each characteristic, at the same dose per kilogram (placebo sessions in the same people)
outcome: Self-rated and physical effects of MDMA (visual analogue scales, 5D-ASC, Adjective Mood Rating Scale, blood pressure, heart rate, temperature, blood level)
magnitude: Unadjusted: blood level and any drug effect beta 0.48. Penalized models: dose per kilogram selected for 21 of 25 responses, first for 12. Adjusted for dose per kilogram: CYP2D6 activity and blood level −0.19 (R2 0.10); age and heart-rate rise −0.27 (R2 0.07); openness and closeness 0.28 (R2 0.08), oceanic boundlessness 0.22 (R2 0.06); neuroticism and trait anxiety and dread of ego dissolution 0.32 each (R2 0.12 and 0.11), impaired control 0.26 each; anxious-depressed and introverted mood before the dose and 5D-ASC anxiety 0.25 and 0.23 (R2 0.06 and 0.05). Sex and previous MDMA use (at most five times): no association after adjustment.

statement: In adults planning to take a classic psychedelic on their own, a better state of mind measured before the drug is associated with a less challenging experience, and in laboratory LSD sessions mood and personality measured before the dose were associated with how the session went; many of the larger associations reported come from people recalling afterwards how they had felt. In the one prospective study outside a laboratory (Haijen et al., 2018; self-selected adults who answered online surveys; of the 379 who reported back, 48% took LSD or 1P-LSD, 29% psilocybin and 11% ayahuasca), feeling comfortable, open, well prepared, not anxious and in a good mood, rated by the participants within the day before ('set'), went with lower Challenging Experience Questionnaire scores they gave about a day after (standardized beta −0.32, SE 0.07, a moderate association), as did recreational or social intentions rated a week before (−0.22, a small one). Strong expectations and a clear intention went with higher mystical-type (0.18) and visual (0.16) scores but not clearly with challenge, and set was unrelated to mystical-type scores. The trait absorption went with more intense experiences of every kind, challenging (0.22) as well as mystical-type (0.35), while trait anxiety, openness, emotional stability, suggestibility and the number of earlier psychedelic experiences were associated with none. The sample shrank from 654 a week before to about 198 in this analysis (editors' inference), and the predictors were adjusted for one another and for an amount the participants estimated after the experience, not for the drug taken or psychiatric history. Average well-being rose from 49.0 before to 52.6 two weeks after, with no comparison group and fewer than half the sample remaining, and mystical-type scores no longer predicted it once traits, intentions and set were in the model. In healthy volunteers given LSD lying in a hospital room, mostly with a placebo session for comparison (nine Basel laboratory studies, 213 people; Vizeli et al., 2024), higher well-being rated on a mood questionnaire just before the dose went with stronger effects on most self-rated scales but not with a bad drug effect, anxiety rated just before with more anxiety during the session, and openness with more mystical-type ratings, at a given dose; the text gives no sizes. In two retrospective online studies, as summarized by a systematic review rated critically low (Aday et al., 2021), states recalled after the experience correlated strongly with it (surrender with mystical-type experience, r = 0.72; preoccupation and confusion with dread, 0.64 and 0.58), and in a US online panel, people who blamed a negative mindset for their most challenging experience rated it as more challenging (beta 0.14) and more often reported thoughts or attempts to hurt themselves or others afterwards (adjusted odds ratio 4.56, 95% CI 2.10 to 9.94; 41 of the 613 reported any; Simonsson et al., 2023). Such recalled states are associations reported by the same people at the same sitting, not predictors. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
plain: People who felt calm, open and ready the day before a trip they had planned rated it as less difficult, and in laboratory LSD sessions feeling well beforehand went with stronger effects and feeling anxious with more anxiety. These links come from watching, not testing, and many people dropped out of the study outside the laboratory. Studies in which people recalled their mood afterwards found bigger links, but memories can be coloured by how the trip went.
population: Adults who use classic psychedelics: people planning their own psychedelic experience who signed up online (one prospective study), healthy volunteers given LSD in laboratory studies, and people recalling past experiences in online surveys
exposure: State of mind, intentions and traits measured before the drug (set within a day before; intentions and traits a week before; mood just before a laboratory dose, personality at screening), and, in retrospective studies, states recalled afterwards
comparator: People with lower or higher scores on each measure within the same study; no study compared people helped to prepare with people who were not
outcome: How challenging, mystical-type or intense the experience was, self-rated (Challenging Experience Questionnaire, Mystical Experience Questionnaire, 5D-ASC, visual analogue scales), and well-being in the following weeks
magnitude: Haijen et al. (2018), standardized coefficients adjusted for one another and for self-estimated amount (about 198 people): set and challenging experience −0.32 (SE 0.07); recreational or social intentions −0.22 (SE 0.08); clear intentions and mystical-type 0.18, visual 0.16, challenging −0.13 (p = 0.088); absorption and challenging 0.22, mystical-type 0.35; R2 0.32 for challenging experience. Vizeli et al. (2024): directions only (no sizes in the text). Recalled afterwards: surrender r = 0.72 with mystical-type experience, preoccupation 0.64 and confusion 0.58 with dread (n = 143, as summarized by Aday et al., 2021); negative mindset blamed for the most challenging experience: beta 0.14, harm thoughts or attempts adjusted OR 4.56 (95% CI 2.10 to 9.94) (Simonsson et al., 2023).

risk_of_bias.note: The prospective study is at high risk of bias (drug type, psychiatric history and other drugs not adjusted; the amount estimated after the experience; about 70% of the baseline sample not in the analysis), the laboratory analysis has some concerns (each predictor adjusted for dose only; no sizes in the text), and the recalled-state findings are at very high risk (attributions made at the same sitting as the outcome) and are worded only as associations (cards sc_haijen_2018, sc_vizeli_2024, sc_aday_2021, sc_simonsson_2023).

inconsistency.note: A worse state of mind or more anxiety measured before the drug goes with a more challenging or anxious experience in both the naturalistic and the laboratory source; absorption's link with mystical and challenging experience alike is reported, not a conflict.

indirectness.note: Worded for the populations studied (self-selected, mostly experienced people planning their own use; screened laboratory volunteers).

imprecision.note: The main prospective coefficient has a standard error of 0.07; for the laboratory analysis only directions are claimed.

publication_bias.note: The review admitted only predictors reported as significant, a file-drawer problem its authors name; the primary studies are cited directly and the review's figures are labelled as summarized.

grade.reasoning: Predictor studies start low, even inside randomized laboratory studies, because the predictors were not randomized; down one for risk of bias, giving very low. Status replicated: a better state of mind measured before the drug went with a less challenging or less anxious experience in two independent sources, one prospective and naturalistic (Imperial College London) and one laboratory (Basel), with different questionnaires, so it is a conceptual replication; the other predictors rest on single studies or on states recalled afterwards. The review (Aday et al., 2021) is used only for what it adds (the retrospective Russ studies and the tabulation of absorption), since its Table 1 misprints the sign for set.

statement: In people who use classic psychedelics, feeling safe and supported is associated with fewer reported difficulties in retrospective surveys, while the one prospective study found only a weak, uncertain link for the place and the people. In that study (Haijen et al., 2018; about 198 self-selected adults planning their own experience), a good feeling about the people who would be present and about the place, rated within the day before, went with slightly lower Challenging Experience Questionnaire scores rated about a day after (standardized beta −0.14, p = 0.070, not statistically significant), and a retreat or a setting designed for therapy, reported afterwards as one yes-or-no item, was associated with no acute measure (0.02); the authors note that the term was not defined for participants. In an international online survey of 6,877 self-selected people who had drunk ayahuasca, each point higher on a 1-to-4 rating of support and safety at their last ceremony went with 0.29 points less extreme fear or panic on a 0-to-10 scale (95% CI 0.15 to 0.43, editors' calculation), slightly fewer difficulties in the weeks after, and current distress lower by 0.62 points on the 40-point Kessler scale, under 2 points across the whole rating (editors' arithmetic), after adjustment for age, sex, education, mental-health diagnoses, times drunk and years since the last drink; the ratings were made looking back by the same people, and averaged near the top of the scale (Perkins et al., 2021). Among 613 US adults in an online panel who had used a classic psychedelic, those who blamed a lack of psychological support for their most challenging experience rated it as more challenging (beta 0.25) and more often reported thoughts or attempts to hurt themselves or others in the days or weeks after (adjusted odds ratio 2.85, 95% CI 1.27 to 6.42; 41 of the 613 reported any); blaming a disagreeable physical environment went with a smaller difference in challenge (0.09) and none in harm thoughts, and blaming the people around with neither (odds ratio for harm thoughts 0.33, 0.11 to 1.01) (Simonsson et al., 2023). Among 163 experienced people recalling two experiences, mostly at home or at a friend's house, those whose experience was at a party, club or festival (24 first and 12 most recent experiences) had higher average challenge scores than the rest (19 against 17 and 31 against 16 per cent of the maximum), a comparison the authors did not test (Palmer and Maynard, 2022). No study compared settings by design. Certainty: very low. Status: mixed.
plain: In surveys, people who felt safe and supported during a trip reported a little less fear and fewer difficulties, but they rated both afterwards. The one study that asked people beforehand found only a weak, uncertain link between feeling good about the place and the people and how the trip went, and no difference for retreats or settings designed for therapy. No study put people in different settings on purpose to compare them.
population: People who use classic psychedelics outside laboratories: adults planning their own experience (one prospective study), people who drink ayahuasca (one international survey), a US online panel and a self-selected survey of experienced people
exposure: The place and the people: feelings about the setting rated the day before; a retreat or therapeutic setting; support and safety at an ayahuasca ceremony rated afterwards; lack of support, a disagreeable place or disagreeable company blamed for the most challenging experience; party, club or festival settings
comparator: People who rated the setting less favourably, did not blame it, or used elsewhere, within each study
outcome: Challenging experience (Challenging Experience Questionnaire), extreme fear or panic, difficulties in the weeks after, thoughts or attempts to hurt oneself or others, and current distress (Kessler-10)
magnitude: Haijen et al. (2018): setting component and challenging experience beta −0.14 (p = 0.070); retreat or therapeutic setting 0.02 (p = 0.81). Perkins et al. (2021), per point of a 1-to-4 support-and-safety rating: extreme fear (0 to 10) −0.29 (95% CI −0.43 to −0.15, editors'), integration difficulties −0.13, Kessler-10 −0.62 (under 2 points across the whole rating). Simonsson et al. (2023), attributions of the most challenging experience: no support beta 0.25, harm thoughts or attempts adjusted OR 2.85 (1.27 to 6.42); disagreeable physical environment 0.09, OR 0.88 (0.33 to 2.35); disagreeable social environment not associated, OR 0.33 (0.11 to 1.01). Palmer and Maynard (2022), untested: party settings 19.27 against 16.77 (first) and 31.46 against 16.16 (most recent) per cent of the maximum CEQ score.

risk_of_bias.note: Retrospective ratings or attributions made by the same people at the same sitting as the outcome, in self-selected samples, with little or no adjustment (very high risk: sc_perkins_2021, sc_simonsson_2023, sc_palmer_2022); the prospective study is at high risk (confounding, heavy attrition) and its retreat item was undefined (sc_haijen_2018).

inconsistency.note: The retrospective surveys point one way, but the prospective study found only a non-significant trend for the setting rating and no association for a retreat or therapeutic setting, and blaming the people around was not associated with challenge in the panel survey.

indirectness.note: Worded for the people and settings studied.

imprecision.note: Large surveys; the prospective coefficient's interval includes zero, which the statement says.

grade.reasoning: Observational evidence starts low; down two for risk of bias and one for inconsistency, giving very low (the floor). Status mixed: four independent studies, the three retrospective ones pointing towards fewer difficulties with more support, the one prospective study only a non-significant trend for the setting and nothing for a retreat or therapeutic setting; recall at the same sitting may explain the difference, but no study has shown that it does.
